raw.directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in groups of 4–6 and thin clumps to 6–9 in apart once established; thinnings are edible. Water regularly and divide crowded clumps every 2–3 years in spring or fall to maintain vigor. Remove spent flower heads to prevent excessive self-seeding, or leave a few for their edible, mildly onion-flavored blooms. Harvest by snipping leaves to about 1 in above the soil; plants regrow quickly.
raw.plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; chives tolerate light frost.

raw.directions: Garlic chives are a hardy perennial allium with flat, grass-like leaves that carry a mild garlic flavor, plus fragrant edible white flowers late in the season. Sow seed in clumps and harvest leaves by snipping from the outside as needed. The star-shaped blooms attract pollinators but self-sow prolifically, so deadhead if you want to limit spread. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.
raw.plant_note: Sow in early spring; clumps return each year and produce edible white flowers.

raw.directions: Unlike French tarragon, Russian tarragon grows readily from seed and forms a vigorous perennial with a milder, anise-like flavor. Surface sow the seed indoors and leave it uncovered under light, then transplant into well-drained soil in full sun. It is hardy, drought tolerant, and grows larger than its French cousin, so give it space at the back of an herb bed. Harvest young leaves for the best flavor and cut plants back to keep them from becoming leggy.
raw.plant_note: Surface sow indoors; light aids germination.

raw.directions: This open-pollinated cilantro produces lush leafy greens and, when it bolts, aromatic coriander seed. Sow directly in cool weather since it bolts quickly once temperatures climb. Make small successive sowings every two to three weeks for a steady leaf harvest. Allow a few plants to flower and set seed to collect coriander or let them self-sow for the next round.
raw.plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather and make successive sowings, since it bolts in summer heat.

raw.directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon balm tolerates more shade than most herbs and is one of the few culinary herbs that produces acceptable quality even in partially shaded sites. Melissa officinalis is a vigorous, lemon-scented European perennial in the mint family producing wrinkled, oval, toothed leaves with a delightful fresh lemon fragrance used in teas, lemonade, salads, fish dishes, poultry, desserts, and liqueurs; it is much milder and more pleasant than lemon verbena for fresh use. Cut plants back hard after flowering to prevent aggressive self-seeding and to stimulate a flush of fresh, fragrant new leaves; in the Gulf South it often dies back in summer heat but re-emerges in fall. Harvest before flowering for best fragrance and flavor.
raw.plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; lemon balm germinates readily in cool soil and grows vigorously in full sun to partial shade, tolerating more shade than most herbs.

raw.directions: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings out, ideally into a buried pot or contained bed, since mint spreads aggressively by runners. Grow it in moist soil and partial to full sun; the aromatic leaves enhance iced tea, mixed drinks, and savory dishes like meats, stews, and vegetable fritters. Cut plants back regularly to encourage tender new growth, and let some tiny flowers bloom to feed the bees.
raw.plant_note: Start indoors and transplant; a vigorous perennial best contained in pots.

raw.directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in a warm, moist seed-starting mix and keep soil above 65°F for reliable sprouting. Pinch out flower buds as soon as they appear to encourage bushy leaf production and delay bolting. Water at the base to avoid fungal spots, and feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer mid-season. Harvest by snipping stems just above a leaf node once plants have at least six true leaves.
raw.plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant only after nights stay reliably above 50°F.

raw.directions: Start the tiny seed indoors, pressing it onto the surface since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into full sun and well-drained soil. This common oregano, also called wild marjoram, has a milder flavor than the pungent Greek type and is the traditional variety for medicinal use. It is a hardy perennial with pretty pink to lavender flowers that draw pollinators; harvest leaves before flowering for the strongest flavor, fresh or dried.
raw.plant_note: Start indoors; surface sow since seed needs light, and transplant out.

raw.directions: Curly parsley is a hardy biennial grown as an annual for its bright green, frilled leaves used as garnish and seasoning. Germination is slow, so soak seed overnight and keep the soil consistently moist. Harvest outer stems first and the plant will keep producing from the center. In milder zones it overwinters and flowers the second year, at which point flavor declines.
raw.plant_note: Sow in early spring; soaking seed overnight speeds notoriously slow germination.

raw.directions: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings into full sun and well-drained soil, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart. This drought-tolerant, hardy perennial has bold, assertive, savory flavor valued for seasoning rich foods like pork, poultry, and cheese, plus stuffing, soups, and stews. It also bears edible purple-blue flowers that draw pollinators; cut plants back in spring to keep them bushy and productive year after year.
raw.plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out; a hardy perennial in most zones.

raw.directions: Rosemary is an aromatic Mediterranean perennial with needle-like leaves that bring a warm, piney flavor to roasts, breads, and herb blends. Start seed indoors ten or more weeks early and be patient, as germination is slow and often spotty. Transplant into sharply drained soil in full sun, since rosemary dislikes wet feet, and water only when the soil dries. In colder climates grow it in a pot and bring it indoors before hard frost, as it is only reliably hardy in mild zones.
raw.plant_note: Start indoors early; germination is slow and erratic.

raw.directions: Surface-sow seeds or cover to 1/8 in in warm, well-drained starting mix; seedlings are small and slow to establish so start early indoors. Plant in sharply drained, lean soil in full sun — like other Mediterranean herbs, thyme deteriorates in fertile, moist conditions. Trim plants lightly after each harvest to prevent woodiness; replace plants every 3–4 years when the center becomes unproductive. Harvest leafy stem tips before or during flowering for the highest thymol content, using fresh or dried in culinary preparations and traditional antiseptic and cough-relief remedies.
raw.plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow or barely cover seed as light aids germination.
